governingDotPoints.text: Classify data as either numerical (discrete or continuous) or categorical (nominal or ordinal) variables

methods.description: Identify the characteristic being described, measured or counted; distinguish it from one recorded value and the person or object, and use the definition to explain why it is a variable.

sourceReview.locator: Stage4 Classify data: statistical variable definition and numerical/categorical boundary
sourceReview.observation: The earliest Stage4 syllabus defines a statistical variable as a characteristic, number or quantity measured or counted and explicitly includes categorical variables. This skill stays at identifying the characteristic/value/person and explaining the definition; no subtype classification or later statistics is assessed.
sourceReview.adjustments: No stage advancement. Retain measured/counted syllabus terms and the original booklet described-characteristic wording for colour.

sourceReview.locator: Classifying Data — complete Variables teaching and age/grade/colour values table
sourceReview.observation: The original Stage4 Variables box explicitly says describe, measure or count and distinguishes Variables from Data Values using age, grade and colour. Its age table is the direct teaching adaptation for example0; its colour row supports example1. There is no separately filled variable-versus-person worked task here, so that part is an elementary adaptation of the definition, not a claimed identical source example.
sourceReview.adjustments: Adapt the age values11,12,15,21,86 to13,17,22 and explicitly ask variable/data value/reason. Adapt the Colour row to a named respondent and favourite-colour response; retain green as a source-supported value. Repair the contradictory omission of described characteristics from Theory and the eye-colour explanation. Do not copy baseline practice cards.

sourceReview.locator: Complete Key Ideas including described/measured/counted variable definition
sourceReview.observation: The complete Key Ideas repeats described/measured/counted. Adjacent broad-type prompts establish a teaching boundary, not permission to expand this definition skill into subtype lessons.
sourceReview.adjustments: Use only the introductory variable definition and familiar wording; do not add numerical/categorical subtype methods.

sourceReview.locator: Complete Foundation question1: contextual measured/counted/described characteristic names
sourceReview.observation: The complete first Foundation question names mass, brand, price, counts and other characteristics, contrasting number and description contexts. Its classification instructions/results are not imported: the present task is identifying the characteristic itself.
sourceReview.adjustments: Use contextual characteristic names as scope/voice evidence only, not as filled examples of identifying variable-versus-person. Good existing assessment values and questions are preserved.

substantiveCorrections.description: Restore original booklet described/measured/counted definition and familiar can-differ wording so categorical responses are supported without claiming every observed value must change.
Remove the contradiction that a non-number characteristic must be measured or counted; explicitly use described/observed eye colour.
Use the height example directly rather than a blanket claim that every variable must exhibit different observed values.
Add two source-table adaptations contrasting measured ages with described colour, one recorded value and the person studied. One actual identification method; no artificial method/example quota.

outcomes.independentSolution: The characteristic recorded for each person is age. 15 years is one recorded age, hence a data value.
outcomes.observation: Both requested identifications are correct; no requirement that every respondent have a different age.

outcomes.independentSolution: Eye colour is the recorded characteristic; brown is one response/data value.
outcomes.observation: A described characteristic qualifies; a number is not required.

outcomes.independentSolution: Number of pets is the family characteristic counted; 3 is one count/data value.
outcomes.observation: The variable is the count characteristic, not an individual observed count.

outcomes.independentSolution: Mass is measured for each student. 47 kg is one measurement/data value.
outcomes.observation: Units are preserved and variable versus value is correctly distinguished.

outcomes.independentSolution: Each player contributes a count of goals. Therefore number of goals scored is the variable; 0,2,1,4 are values of it.
outcomes.observation: Zero is a legitimate count and all supplied values remain data values.

outcomes.independentSolution: The recorded feature is favourite sport. Soccer, netball and tennis are individual responses to that feature.
outcomes.observation: The categorical variable is supported by the described-characteristic source definition.

outcomes.independentSolution: Height is a measurable characteristic of a person; people can have different heights, so it is a statistical variable.
outcomes.observation: The ordinary height context explains measurement and potential variation; identical values in one dataset would not erase the variable.

outcomes.independentSolution: Eye colour can be described/observed and recorded for each person, with possible different responses. It is therefore a statistical variable although not numerical.
outcomes.observation: The repaired wording matches the original described/measured/counted definition and resolves the prior numeric-only contradiction.

outcomes.independentSolution: The 30 students are the individuals studied. Shoe size is the characteristic recorded about each, hence the variable.
outcomes.observation: The sample count is not confused with a variable or a value.

outcomes.independentSolution: James is the person; 15 years is his recorded value; age is the characteristic/variable.
outcomes.observation: All three roles are distinguished correctly.

outcomes.independentSolution: Age is recorded for each person; 15 years is one age value. The variable is age.
outcomes.observation: Only option0 answers the stem; all three wrong-option reasons describe their actual roles.

options.observation: Age names the characteristic recorded.
15 years is one data value, not the characteristic.
The people are the individuals surveyed, not the recorded characteristic.
The survey is the collection process, not the variable.

outcomes.independentSolution: The characteristic counted for each student is number of books borrowed; 3,0,5,2 are its recorded values.
outcomes.observation: Only option0 is the variable; the highest value5 remains a value, not a distinct variable.

options.observation: Number of books borrowed is the characteristic counted.
3,0,5,2 is a list of values, not the characteristic name.
Students are the individuals studied.
5 books is one recorded count, the largest in the list, not the characteristic.

outcomes.independentSolution: Height can be measured and can differ between people. It therefore fits the statistical-variable definition.
outcomes.observation: The repaired everyone-same-height reason addresses this concrete height context without defining a variable as mandatory observed variation.

options.observation: Measurement and potential difference correctly justify height as a variable.
One person’s reading is a data value; being a single reading does not define the variable.
Everyone having the same height is not generally true and does not explain the measurable characteristic. A particular equal-valued dataset would still have height as its variable.
Height need not be a whole number; measured values and non-numerical characteristics are allowed.

outcomes.independentSolution: Shoe size is recorded for each of the30 students, so shoe size is the variable.
outcomes.observation: All option reasons correctly separate individuals, collection method and one response.

options.observation: Shoe size is the characteristic being recorded.
The30 students are individuals, not the variable.
The survey is the collection method.
Size8 is one shoe-size value, not the characteristic itself.

outcomes.independentSolution: Favourite sport is the feature recorded. Soccer/netball/tennis are responses; the students are individuals.
outcomes.observation: Only option0 names the variable; listed categories are values rather than a different assessed method.

options.observation: Favourite sport is the described characteristic.
Soccer is one response/data value.
Students answering are the individuals.
The three sports are some possible recorded values, not the characteristic name.

outcomes.independentSolution: (a) Age. (b)13,17 or22 years is a valid data value;17 years is the supplied correct choice. (c) Age can be measured and can differ between people.
outcomes.observation: Every requested part is answered; the source Age table is adapted without pretending it is a filled identical source worked task. Distinct13/17/22 values are manageable and no arithmetic shortcut is introduced.

outcomes.independentSolution: Variable=favourite colour; one value=green; person=Nora. It is a variable because colour preference can be described and responses can differ.
outcomes.observation: This is the categorical/person contrast to example0, supported by the original Colour row and definition; no subtype classification or advanced statistics is imported.

review.theoryObservation: Current intro/facts correctly allow described, measured or counted characteristics and distinguish the characteristic, one data value and the person. Potential difference is expressed with can rather than mandatory distinct observations. No Theory.steps exists, so no procedure-header repair or invented steps judgement is needed. All17 solution texts are coherent with this teaching. The one identify-statistical-variable method is mapped to every assessment and both examples; the measured-age and described-colour examples cover its actual contrasts without quota padding. The retained4/4/2 practice and5quiz narrow bank is adequate for this introductory atom.
review.sourceObservation: Read all four complete hash-bound sections: Stage4 syllabus2612–2617; original DataVisualisation Variables44–67, KeyIdeas175–192 and Foundation196–218. The original definition explicitly includes describe/measure/count, and its Age/Grade/Colour table supports both numerical and described data values. The source Foundation contextual names support ordinary language only; its classification task is not falsely presented as a filled variable/person example. Scope stays at introductory identification/explanation, excludes neighbouring numerical/categorical subtypes and unrelated algebra/rates. Author source adjustments accurately acknowledge elementary adaptation; no original source images or missing-image waivers occur in these selected spans.
